title: Wolfgang Amadeus Mozart's Life In Reverse | From a Vienna Grave to a Salzburg Baptism
description:
Mozart's life runs backwards in this episode, opening with his death in Vienna in 1791 and rewinding to his baptism in Salzburg in 1756. The journey steps through the mass he left unfinished when he died, the opera premiered to a paying house in September 1791, the loan letters he wrote to a fellow mason and the first dances his father wrote down when he was five. Every scene moves to an earlier year, so the music arrives in reverse order and the money behind it comes into view. Dates, places and premieres follow the documented record, and the stories told later about him are reported as stories.

scenes.narration: A bronze statue of him stands in a garden in Vienna where the court used to walk, and the house he was born in at Salzburg is a museum with his name over the door. His face has been printed on money and used in advertising, and the town he ran away from now trades on the name he gave it.

He died at home in Vienna on December 5, 1791, at the age of thirty-five, after about a fortnight in bed. The doctors who attended him wrote down a sudden fever, and the cause has been argued over by physicians and biographers ever since. His wife was ill in bed herself and could not sit with him.

He was buried the next day at the St. Marx cemetery outside the city. The rules of the time in Vienna meant the grave was opened for re-use after a term of years and given no lasting marker, and the ground has been disturbed since, so the exact place is not known for certain.

In the second half of November 1791 he took to his bed and did not get up. Swelling of the limbs was noted by those who visited, and a doctor was called more than once. He kept asking after the parts of the unfinished mass, and friends reported that he was calm through the bad nights.

He had been commissioned to write a funeral mass in the spring of 1791 by a nobleman who intended to use it for his wife's memorial and had a habit of putting his own name on other men's work. He was still adding to it when the illness stopped him. His pupil was given the sketches that winter and completed them.

On September 30, 1791, a comic play with singing, machines and a magic flute was given for the first time at a theatre in the Wieden, a suburb of Vienna. The house was his own, the manager sang the bird catcher, and the tickets were priced for working people. It played through the winter and was still running when he died.

Three weeks before that, on September 6, 1791, an opera on an old Roman story was performed in Prague for the coronation of a new emperor, with the composer in the city conducting. The Czechs had taken to his music years earlier, and they received this one well. He was paid for it and left for home.

In the autumn of 1790 he went to Frankfurt for the coronation of the emperor, with the hope of new work in the north. He played at a public concert during the week of the ceremony, was paid, and returned to Vienna with nothing permanent settled. He had already been in Vienna twelve years by then.

Through 1789 and 1790 he wrote repeatedly to a man in his own lodge of masons asking for loans, and the letters set out plainly what he owed and what he could not cover. He taught pupils in the mornings, played at benefits, and still fell behind. The books kept after his death showed a house in debt.

In the spring of 1789 the king of Prussia invited him to Berlin and kept him for some weeks, hearing him play and asking for works for the court musicians. He was paid well and came home at the end of June. The visit brought money at a moment when money was short, and no post.

In the summer of 1788 he wrote three symphonies in as many months, sending for money from his landlord and neighbours in the same weeks. A series of concerts was planned to play them in Vienna, and no record of those performances has ever been found, which leaves the question open. The three are among the last he wrote.

At the end of 1787 the emperor appointed him court composer with a salary for writing dances to be played at the imperial balls. He had been asked twice for money already that year and had given his word that he would work his way out of trouble. The post covered the household for a while.

On May 28, 1787, his father died in Salzburg, in the same weeks that his new opera was filling the theatre in Vienna. The two men had written to each other for years about money, employment and obedience, and the tone of the letters is well known. He stayed in Vienna and did not go back for the burial.

A comedy about a servant who outwits his master was performed for the first time on May 1, 1787, at the court theatre in Vienna. It ran several times that season and the composer was paid for it, but the theatre did not keep it in the program as long as he expected.

In February 1785 he printed six string quartets in Vienna and dedicated them to Joseph Haydn, the man he had studied under as a boy. He took them round to him. Haydn wrote to the father in Salzburg that he knew of no composer like his son, and the letter is kept in the family papers.

His father came up from Salzburg in the same winter to stay for three months, hearing the new music and looking at how his son lived. The visit covered the printing of the quartets and a round of concerts. It was the last long time they spent together, and the letters after it turn on money and the future.

In the season of 1784 and 1785 he gave a series of subscription concerts in Vienna, playing new concertos from the keyboard and directing the players from the same chair. The city had a fashion for them and he had to keep writing for them. Most of the concertos he performed in those years he wrote himself.

He married on August 4, 1782, in Vienna, a woman from a family he had known for years and whom his father had warned him against. He had written for permission and the answer was slow and reluctant. They had children early, and of the children born in the following years only two sons lived to grow up.

On Christmas Eve 1781 the emperor put him up against an English pianist who had just arrived in Vienna, and both were asked to play and to improvise. The court watched, and the evening was written about afterwards. He was twenty-five, in the emperor's city, and had already left the service of his own archbishop.

In June 1781 he was told by the archbishop's steward in Vienna that he was no longer required, and he did not go home to Salzburg as a servant again. He stayed in the city, giving lessons, playing in houses and waiting for opera work to come. The break with the employer his father served cost the family four years of argument.

Back in Salzburg in 1779 he was taken on at the archbishop's court in a salaried post that gave him organ duties and the writing of church music. The salary was fixed and the work was set. He had been abroad looking for something better for two years and had found nothing, so he resumed the place he had.

In July 1778 his mother died in Paris, in a room they had shared while he looked for work. She was buried in a common grave and no one knows where. He was twenty-two, he had failed to find a post in two countries, and he wrote to his father in pieces, keeping the worst news back until he had to send it.

He had set out from Salzburg in August 1777 with his mother and his sister to look for employment at the courts of Germany, and the search ran through Mannheim, where he fell in love with a singer who would not have him, and on to Paris. The archbishop had refused him leave to travel on his own, and he went anyway.

In the autumn of 1771 he wrote an opera for a princely wedding at Milan and the city liked it enough to order another. He was fifteen. Italy had already taken him twice, and the commissions there were the best his father could find for a boy whose Salzburg employers wanted church music and nothing else.

On a visit to Rome in 1770, at fourteen, he was taken into the papal chapel to hear the setting sung there on Good Friday, and his father wrote home that the boy wrote it out from memory after one hearing. The pope received him in the same journey and made him a knight. Both details come down to us in family letters.

In October 1769 he and his father left Salzburg for Italy for the first of three journeys that filled most of three years. They travelled by coach, the boy slept on the seats, and he wrote letters home from every stopping place. Between them they were working out whether any court in Europe would take him.

By the time he was twelve he had written short stage works that were performed at the archbishop's palace in Salzburg and in Vienna, each one written for a specific singer and a specific room. The emperor heard one of them. His father printed the pieces to sell, and the family lived between the court and the market for music.

In the autumn of 1762 his father took him and his sister to Munich and then to Vienna, where the children played for the imperial family and their father wrote home at length about the welcome they received. The children were dressed for it, the courts paid, and the tour was the family's business.

In 1761, at five, he was writing short dances and minuets that his father took and set down in a notebook he kept for the children's music, with the dates written beside them. His sister played too, and the two of them performed for visitors while their father, a violinist at the court, took the fee.

He was born on January 27, 1756, in the house on the main street of Salzburg, and was christened the next day at the nearest church. He was the last of seven children and only one sister was still living. His father was a violinist at the archbishop's court who that same year printed a book on how to play the instrument.
